subject: English
passage: Writings by the Kyoto School—an influential collective of Japanese philosophers active in Kyoto during the 1920s and '40s—are recognizable by their reiteration of the same general conceptual frameworks and concerns: nothingness (mu) and absolute contradictory self-identity, to name two. But there was room for individuation: Keiji Nishitani's Religion and Nothingness, for example, may resemble other Kyoto School works at first glance, but his writings stand out for their comparative existential urgency and integration of Western philosophy.
prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It explains how a particular group of thinkers began collaborating and then recounts how one member of that group became especially influential among them.
choices.B: It describes the common perception that a particular group of thinkers' works are derivative and then provides a specific piece of evidence that reinforces that perception.
choices.C: It describes an intellectual framework shared by a particular group of thinkers and then makes and illustrates the claim that individuals introduced variations within that framework.
choices.D: It offers historical context that accounts for a particular group of thinkers' shared approach and then indicates the circumstances under which several members of that group began exploring more unconventional methods.

explanation: Choice C is the best answer because it accurately describes the text's two-part structure. First, the passage establishes that Kyoto School writings share common features: they are 'recognizable by their reiteration of the same general conceptual frameworks and concerns,' including 'nothingness (mu) and absolute contradictory self-identity.' The text then transitions with 'But there was room for individuation' to make the claim that individuals introduced variations within this framework, and illustrates this with Nishitani's example—his writings 'stand out for their comparative existential urgency and integration of Western philosophy' while still resembling other Kyoto School works.
